In our internal immunotherapy cohort, CIPHER consistently distinguished patients at elevated risk of ICI-P from those without the event, with AUCs ranging from 0.77 to 0.85. In head-to-head benchmarking, CIPHER achieved an AUC of 0.83, outperforming the clinical, radiomics and ensemble models. In the external validation cohort, CIPHER maintained high performance (AUC=0.83; balanced accuracy=81.7%), exceeding the radiomics model (DeLong p=0.0318) and demonstrating superior specificity without sacrificing sensitivity. By contrast, the radiomics model, despite high sensitivity (85.0%), showed markedly lower specificity (45.8%). Confusion matrix analyses confirmed CIPHER’s robust classification, correctly identifying 80 of 96 non–ICI-P cases and 16 of 20 ICI-P cases.

Conclusions

We developed and externally validated CIPHER, a CT-based imaging biomarker for pretreatment ICI-P risk stratification in NSCLC. CIPHER shows promise as a noninvasive tool for ICI-P risk assessment but warrants prospective validation before clinical translation.

Highlights

The first chest CT AI foundation model for immune toxicity – We introduce CIPHER (Checkpoint-Inhibitor Pneumonitis Hazard EstimatoR), a transformer-based masked autoencoder trained through self-supervised contrastive learning on 590,284 CT slices from 4,242 CT scans from NSCLC patients. This large-scale pretraining enables CIPHER to learn intrinsic lung parenchymal representations linked to immune toxicity risk. Robust validation and benchmarking – We fine-tuned and evaluated CIPHER across independent internal and external NSCLC immunotherapy cohorts, achieving AUCs of 0.77–0.85 internal and 0.83 external testing, surpassing comparator models in both performance and generalizability. Interpretability and translational potential – We demonstrate how model-derived attention maps align with clinically relevant pulmonary patterns, enhancing interpretability. Translational potential – CIPHER’s performance and scalability underscore its potential as a decision-support tool to guide treatment planning, pre-emptive monitoring, and toxicity mitigation in immunotherapy practice.

Background

TFE3-rearranged renal cell carcinoma (TFE3-rRCC) is a rare, aggressive subtype that predominantly affects adolescents and young adults. Its marked morphologic heterogeneity can delay recognition and downstream confirmatory testing.

Methods

We assembled a two-center retrospective cohort of patients < 30 years with renal cell carcinoma (n = 228; 59 TFE3-rRCC), using fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) as the reference standard. Model development was performed in a development cohort (n = 129), followed by independent external validation (n = 99). We developed TFE3-DualNet, an ensemble of weakly supervised CLAM models trained on routine hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) whole-slide images (WSIs) using patch embeddings extracted from two pathology foundation models (UNI and CHIEF). We compared performance with three immunohistochemistry (IHC) scoring methods and a feature-fusion CLAM baseline using concatenated H&E-derived UNI and CHIEF features, and assessed interpretability by attention mapping.

Results

In the external validation cohort, TFE3-DualNet achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.932, with accuracy 0.879, sensitivity 0.893, and specificity 0.873. The model outperformed IHC scoring methods (AUROC 0.793-0.819; all p < 0.05) and exceeded the feature-fusion baseline (AUROC 0.906). Attention hotspots localized to diagnostically relevant tumor regions and showed concordance with TFE3 IHC patterns.

Conclusions

TFE3-DualNet showed encouraging performance as an interpretable H&E WSI-based screening model for TFE3-rRCC in young patients, supporting its potential use to prioritize confirmatory testing and pathologist review in routine diagnostic workflows.

An Evaluation of DMR-Informed Fine-Tuning of Tissue Array–Pretrained CpGPT for Gastrointestinal Cancer Classification Using cfDNA Targeted Methylation

Background

Cell-free DNA (cfDNA) methylation profiling is promising for minimally invasive cancer detection, but its translation is limited by high-dimensional data, modest cfDNA cohort sizes, and the difficulty of defining biologically grounded feature sets. CpGPT, a transformer-based DNA methylation foundation model pretrained on large-scale tissue methylation array datasets, may enable transfer of learned methylation representations to data-limited cfDNA applications. We evaluated a differentially methylated region (DMR)-informed framework for fine-tuning CpGPT for gastrointestinal cancer classification using plasma cfDNA methylation data.

Methods

Plasma cfDNA methylation data were obtained from the EpiPanGI Dx cohort, including 254 gastrointestinal cancer samples and 46 non-cancer controls. Tumor and matched normal tissue methylation data included 967 tumor-normal pairs across 18 cancer types from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA). Tissue-derived and cfDNA-derived DMRs were identified independently and intersected to define a candidate set of 20,499 CpG sites. CpGPT was evaluated in a technical sensitivity analysis using the previously published 896-CpG panGI panel and in DMR-informed fine-tuning using the 20,499-CpG candidate set. Performance was compared with radial-kernel support vector machine (SVM radial), elastic net logistic regression, gradient boosting machine (GBM), and Random Forest models using identical data partitions.

Results

In the technical sensitivity analysis using the previously published panGI panel, the CpGPT base configuration achieved a mean test area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.9799 (95% CI, 0.9654–0.9944) across four fixed random seeds. Individual test AUROCs ranged from 0.9597 to 0.9927, while neighboring configurations achieved mean test AUROCs of 0.9661–0.9716. Using the DMR-informed candidate set, CpGPT achieved a mean test AUROC of 0.9904 (95% CI, 0.9715–1.0000) across three split-runs. Mean test AUROCs were 0.9573 for SVM radial, 0.9420 for elastic net, 0.8460 for GBM, and 0.8408 for Random Forest. Cancer type-specific mean test AUROCs ranged from 0.9600 for pancreatic adenocarcinoma to 1.0000 for esophageal squamous cell carcinoma, colorectal cancer, and esophageal adenocarcinoma.

Conclusions

DMR-informed CpGPT fine-tuning achieved high internal discrimination and a higher mean test AUROC than the evaluated classical machine learning models. Integrating tissue and plasma cfDNA methylation evidence provides a biologically constrained feature space for adapting a tissue array-pretrained foundation model to cfDNA classification. Independent external validation, clinically representative control populations, and further feature-set reduction are needed before translation into a targeted cfDNA assay.

Predicting pathological complete response (pCR) to neoadjuvant immunochemotherapy in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) is clinically important yet remains challenging. We then fine-tuned a lung cancer-specific CT foundation model from a pretrained 3D model (VoCo) using 6643 chest CT scans. Finally, we constructed a multi-task Swin Transformer that jointly performs risk stratification and segments tumors to generate the imaging biomarker. Across five centers, the model achieved consistently strong generalization (AUC: 0.75-0.87) for pCR prediction. Cancer drug response (CDR) prediction is challenging due to tumor heterogeneity and limited amount of high-quality response data. Spatial proteomics technologies have transformed our understanding of complex tissue architecture in cancer but present unique challenges for computational analysis<sup>1</sup>. Prediction of acute postoperative protein depletion risk in colon cancer using an in-context learning foundation model: a retrospective cohort study.

Background

Acute postoperative protein depletion, including hypoalbuminaemia and hypoproteinaemia, frequently complicates colon cancer surgery and exacerbates adverse outcomes, yet early risk stratification remains challenging.

Aims

To develop a predictive model utilising a tabular foundation model for acute postoperative protein depletion in colon cancer patients, alongside an interpretable clinical web tool.

Methods

We retrospectively evaluated perioperative data from 812 colon cancer patients treated between 2020 and 2025. Following recursive feature elimination, eight traditional machine learning algorithms and the TabICLv2 tabular foundation model were trained. Discrimination, calibration, incremental risk stratification, and clinical utility were assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), paired DeLong tests, calibration curves, Brier score, net reclassification improvement (NRI), integrated discrimination improvement (IDI), and decision curve analysis. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) were used to visualise feature contributions.

Results

TabICLv2 achieved the numerically highest validation AUC among the evaluated algorithms using nine selected predictors, with an AUC of 0.766 (95% CI: 0.699-0.832) and a Brier score of 0.158. DeLong tests showed no statistically significant AUC differences between TabICLv2 and XGBoost or Random Forest. NRI/IDI analyses indicated improved event reclassification across comparator models, with significant total NRI and IDI improvement over Random Forest, whereas incremental improvement over Logistic Regression and XGBoost was limited. Sensitivity analyses using albumin-only and total-protein-only endpoints showed broadly consistent discrimination. SHAP analysis revealed age, prealbumin (PA), and globulin (GLO) as the leading contributors to model predictions. A web-based calculator was subsequently deployed to facilitate clinical translation. Conclusion: TabICLv2 integrates demographic, nutritional, and immunological profiles to predict acute postoperative protein depletion with moderate discrimination. The accompanying application may provide adjunctive individualised risk assessment, but prospective multicentre validation is required before routine clinical implementation.

Foundation Model-empowered Multimodal Prediction of Platinum Resistance in High-grade Serous Ovarian Cancer: A Multicenter Retrospective Study.

Rationale and objectives

To develop and validate a foundation model (FM)-empowered multimodal framework to predict platinum resistance in patients with high-grade serous ovarian cancer (HGSOC).

Materials and methods

This multicenter retrospective cohort study included 744 HGSOC patients who underwent primary debulking surgery across four centers. Perioperative multimodal data were collected, including clinical variables, preoperative pelvic magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and postoperative hematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-stained whole slide images (WSIs). Pretrained radiology and pathology FMs were used as frozen feature extractors, and attention-based aggregation was applied to summarize variable-length MRI slices and WSI tiles. A cross-modal fusion module integrated modalities and supported missing-modality inference. Model performance was evaluated using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) and compared with late-fusion (LF) baselines.

Results

In the internal validation cohort, unimodal and multimodal FM variants achieved AUCs ranging from 0.708 to 0.780, and in external test cohorts A, B, and C achieved AUCs ranging from 0.653 to 0.790. The trimodal FM (clinical+MRI+WSI) achieved the highest AUC in all cohorts (internal validation: 0.780; external cohorts A, B, and C: 0.779, 0.781, and 0.790, respectively), outperforming the trimodal LF model (internal validation: 0.753; external cohorts A, B, and C: 0.729, 0.715, and 0.730, respectively).

Conclusion

A FM-empowered multimodal model integrating clinical, MRI, and pathological data was constructed to predict platinum resistance in HGSOC, demonstrating superior and stable performance across centers.

GutCore: An Endoscopy Foundation Model for Whole-Case Gastric Cancer Analysis

Background

Routine endoscopy image sets contain complementary information about lesions, surrounding mucosa, anatomy, and examination context. However, most endoscopic artificial intelligence systems are developed and evaluated on selected frames for narrowly defined image-level tasks, limiting their ability to support case-level analysis.

Objective

To develop GutCore, an endoscopy foundation model for whole-case patient-level gastric cancer analysis, and assess whether routinely stored endoscopic image sets can support cancer detection, invasion-depth prediction, biomarker inference, and prognosis.

Design

GutCore was pretrained on 5.6 million de-identified endoscopic images from more than ten hospitals. We compared GutCore with general, medical, and endoscopy-specific foundation models using public image-level datasets and an internal retrospective cohort of 11,035 de-identified endoscopic examinations from Samsung Medical Center (2019–2023). Whole-case image sets were aggregated for patient-level prediction of cancer status, invasion depth, biomarker status, and overall survival.

Results

GutCore achieved AUCs of 0.996 for cancer detection, 0.960 for muscularis propria invasion, 0.801 for SM2-or-deeper invasion, and 0.781 for mucosal versus submucosal invasion among ESD-treated early gastric cancer cases. Biomarker prediction was strongest for EBV status and MLH1 loss and weaker for HER2 status, with AUCs of 0.861, 0.822, and 0.648, respectively. In the held-out advanced gastric cancer test set, GutCore-derived risk groups separated overall survival (log-rank P < .0001; high-risk vs low-risk hazard ratio, 13.18; 95% CI, 6.06–28.66), including within pathological stage II and III disease. Public image-level benchmarks further supported the generality of the learned endoscopic representation.

Conclusions

GutCore enabled whole-case patient-level gastric cancer assessment from routinely stored endoscopic images, extending endoscopy foundation model evaluation beyond selected frames. Independent external validation is required before clinical use.

Background Foundation models show promise in medical imaging but remain underexplored in three-dimensional modalities. Despite the adoption of digital breast tomosynthesis (DBT) in breast cancer screening, no dedicated foundation model currently exists for this modality. Purpose To develop and evaluate a foundation model for DBT (DBT-DINO) and assess the impact of domain-specific pretraining across multiple clinical tasks. Materials and Methods This retrospective study used DBT images from Mass General Brigham acquired between March 2011 and February 2024. Self-supervised pretraining was performed using Meta AI's DINOv2 methodology on more than 25 million two-dimensional sections from 487 975 DBT volumes from 27 990 patients. Three downstream tasks were evaluated: (a) breast density classification using 5000 screening examinations, (b) 5-year risk of developing biopsy-proven breast cancer using 106 417 screening examinations, and (c) lesion detection using 393 annotated volumes. The performance of DBT-DINO was compared with that of ImageNet-pretrained DINOv2 baselines using McNemar and DeLong tests. Results A total of 4981 patients (mean age, 57.76 years ± 11.40 [SD]; 4855 female) were included for density classification, 31 561 patients (mean age, 60.09 years ± 10.47; 31 559 female) were included for risk prediction, and 199 female patients were included for lesion detection. For breast density classification, DBT-DINO achieved 79% (786 of 997 examinations) accuracy, outperforming the DINOv2 baseline (73% [728 of 997 examinations]; P < .001). For 5-year breast cancer risk prediction, DBT-DINO had an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.78 and DINOv2 had an AUC of 0.76 (P = .057), showing no evidence of a difference. In lesion detection, DINOv2 had an average sensitivity of 67% (91 of 136 lesions), whereas DBT-DINO had a sensitivity of 62% (84 of 136 lesions) (P = .60), again with no evidence of a difference. Conclusion DBT-DINO demonstrated strong performance in breast density classification; however, there was no evidence of a difference compared with the ImageNet baseline in 5-year breast cancer risk prediction or lesion detection, suggesting that domain-specific pretraining for localized detection tasks required further refinement. © RSNA, 2026 Supplemental material is available for this article. evidence_text: Nicheformer: a foundation model for single-cell and spatial omics. Tissue makeup depends on the local cellular microenvironment. Spatial single-cell genomics enables scalable and unbiased interrogation of these interactions. Here we introduce Nicheformer, a transformer-based foundation model trained on both human and mouse dissociated single-cell and targeted spatial transcriptomics data. Pretrained on SpatialCorpus-110M, a curated collection of over 57 million dissociated and 53 million spatially resolved cells across 73 tissues on cellular reconstruction, Nicheformer learns cell representations that capture spatial context. Nicheformer enables the prediction of the spatial context of dissociated cells, allowing the transfer of rich spatial information to scRNA-seq datasets. Overall, Nicheformer sets the stage for the next generation of machine-learning models in spatial single-cell analysis.

A Melanoma Brain Metastasis CTC Signature and CTC:B-cell Clusters Associate with Secondary Liver Metastasis: A Melanoma Brain-Liver Metastasis Axis.

Abstract

Melanoma brain metastasis is linked to dismal prognosis and low overall survival and is detected in up to 80% of patients at autopsy. Circulating tumor cells (CTC) are the smallest functional units of cancer and precursors of fatal metastasis. We previously used an unbiased multilevel approach to discover a unique ribosomal protein large/small subunit (RPL/RPS) CTC gene signature associated with melanoma brain metastasis. In this study, we hypothesized that CTC-driven melanoma brain metastasis secondary metastasis (“metastasis of metastasis” per clinical scenarios) has targeted organ specificity for the liver. We injected parallel cohorts of immunodeficient and newly developed humanized NBSGW (huNBSGW) mice with cells from CTC-derived melanoma brain metastasis to identify secondary metastatic patterns. We found the presence of a melanoma brain–liver metastasis axis in huNBSGW mice. Furthermore, RNA sequencing analysis of tissues showed a significant upregulation of the RPL/RPS CTC gene signature linked to metastatic spread to the liver. Additional RNA sequencing of CTCs from huNBSGW blood revealed extensive CTC clustering with human B cells in these mice. CTC:B-cell clusters were also upregulated in the blood of patients with primary melanoma and maintained either in CTC-driven melanoma brain metastasis or melanoma brain metastasis CTC–derived cells promoting liver metastasis. CTC-generated tumor tissues were interrogated at single-cell gene and protein expression levels (10x Genomics Xenium and HALO spatial biology platforms, respectively). Collectively, our findings suggest that heterotypic CTC:B-cell interactions can be critical at multiple stages of metastasis.

Significance

This study provides important insights into the relevance of prometastatic CTC:B-cell clusters in melanoma progression, extends the importance of the CTC RPL/RPS gene signature beyond primary metastasis/melanoma brain metastasis driving targeted organ specificity for liver metastasis ("metastasis of metastasis"), and identifies new targets for clinical melanoma metastasis therapies.

Characterizing cell-type-specific spatially variable genes (SVGs) within tissue context is essential for exploring the landscape of complex biological systems in spatial transcriptomic (ST) studies. In this paper, we present a unified framework, the Mixture of Mixed Models (MMM), designed to directly model RNA count data and identify cell-type-specific SVGs while accounting for cell type composition and correcting for platform effects. Through a comprehensive simulation study and the analyses of eight publicly available ST datasets from various tissues and technologies with different resolutions, we demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of MMM in identifying cell-type-specific SVGs. Notably, our integrative analysis with genome-wide association studies reveals that the cell-type-specific SVGs identified by MMM in a mouse brain study exhibit significant heritability enrichment in brain-related phenotypes. Spatial transcriptomic (ST) technologies ( 1 – 8 ) enable the measurement of gene expression and physical locations simultaneously, providing unprecedented opportunities to reveal the diversity and complexity of biological systems within the tissue context ( 9 ,  10 ). To fully harness the power of ST technologies, it is crucial to characterize spatially variable genes (SVGs) ( 11 – 14 ) in a cell-type-specific manner—essentially, how the gene expression changes across space within a cell type of interest. The cell-type-specific SVGs may exhibit distinct spatial patterns such as clustering and periodicity, reflecting different cell states. These spatial patterns can be attributed to particular tissue structures or local microenvironment niches and indicate certain biological processes in various contexts ( 15 ), including functional programs, pathogenic processes ( 16 ), cell–cell communications ( 17 – 19 ), and tumor ecosystems ( 8 ,  20 ). Further investigations into the cell-type-specific SVGs have great potential to advance our understanding of the mechanisms underlying complex diseases ( 16 ,  21 ), and subsequently help identify potential therapeutic targets.  However, the current limitations of ST technologies present several challenges in characterizing cell-type-specific SVGs. First, cell type composition is a major confounding factor in practice ( 15 ). As the composition of cell types varies spatially, the expression of their marker genes also changes accordingly. Without effectively accounting for this confounding factor, the SVGs identified by most existing methods, such as SpatialDE ( 22 ), SPARK ( 23 ), SPARK-X ( 24 ), and HEARTSVG ( 25 ), may simply be marker genes of a cell type rather than cell-type-specific SVGs. In the ST data with low resolution, such as Slide-seq ( 3 ) and 10x Visium ( 4 ), the gene expression measurements at spatial spots originate from mixtures of multiple cells. Although cell type deconvolution ( 26 ,  27 ) can provide estimates of cell type proportions at each spot, the presence of cell type mixtures complicates the identification of cell-type-specific SVGs. Even in high-resolution ST data like MERFISH ( 1 ), Stereo-seq ( 6 ), 10x Xenium ( 7 ), and 10x Visium HD ( 8 ), uncertainties in cell type identification persist due to diffusion or imperfect cellular segmentation ( 15 ), and overlooking this uncertainty can lead to inflated type I errors and unreplicable results. Second, single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) data are often used as the reference for cell type deconvolution and identification in ST studies. However, the expression profiles observed in ST data may not fully align with scRNA-seq reference data due to platform differences ( 26 ). Without accounting for the platform effects, spurious spatial variations in ST data might be misidentified as SVGs. Third, the expression patterns of cell-type-specific SVGs in real data remain largely unknown and possibly diverse, posing a challenge for using parametric methods that may have limited statistical power. There is still a need for the development of flexible methodologies capable of addressing these challenges and capturing a wide spectrum of spatial patterns.  In this paper, we introduce a unified statistical framework called Mixture of Mixed Models (MMM), standing for the Mixture of Mixed Models, to identify cell-type-specific SVGs. The success of MMM relies on its probabilistic model, which accounts for cell type composition and corrects for platform effects between ST and scRNA-seq data explicitly. In the MMM framework, cell-type-specific gene expression in ST data is decomposed into three components: the average gene expression of the same cell type obtained from scRNA-seq reference data, spatial variations, and nonspatial variations. The statistical significance of spatial variations is examined using a powerful nonparametric test ( 23 ,  28 ) capable of detecting diverse spatial patterns. While methods such as CTSV ( 29 ), C-SIDE ( 15 ), spVC ( 30 ), Celina ( 31 ), and STANCE ( 32 ) can be used to identify cell-type-specific SVGs, MMM achieves superior performance that benefits from our innovations in model and algorithm design (detailed comparison in   SI Appendix ,  Methods  ). Through a comprehensive simulation study, we showed that MMM can produce well-calibrated    P   -values; thus, it can effectively control type I errors and achieve high statistical power. We then applied MMM to eight publicly available ST datasets of different tissues from various species. These datasets were generated by different platforms with a wide range of resolutions, including 10x Visium ( 4 ), Spatial Transcriptomics ( 2 ), 10x Xenium ( 7 ), 10x Visium HD ( 8 ), and Stereo-seq ( 6 ). In our study of the mouse brain, we demonstrated that MMM can identify cell-type-specific SVGs that are replicable across different technologies. We further conducted an integrative analysis with genome-wide association studies (GWASs) and found that the identified cell-type-specific SVGs are significantly enriched in brain-related phenotypes. This suggests that MMM has great potential to elucidate the mechanisms underlying complex traits and diseases. We also used MMM to analyze a high-resolution Xenium human breast cancer dataset by accounting for the uncertainties from imperfect cell segmentation and annotation, showing that certain cell-type-specific SVGs given by MMM may contribute to cell–cell communications and regulate the tissue microenvironment. Furthermore, we applied MMM to the 3D tissue models constructed from multiple ST slices, demonstrating its utility in 3D data analysis.   Results   Method Overview.  Given the common presence of cell type mixtures across space in the spatially resolved transcriptomic data, identifying cell-type-specific SVGs requires not only separating the contributions of different cell types from overall gene expression measurements but also inferring whether each contribution varies across spatial locations. This appears to be a challenging task; however, with the rapid advancement of cell type deconvolution methods ( 26 ,  27 ,  33 ,  34 ), their reliable performance offers opportunities to explore cell-type-specific signals. Hence, we propose a probabilistic framework called MMM that enables the statistical characterization of cell-type-specific SVGs by accounting for the cell type mixtures in the spatial context.  Specifically, we begin the model design with raw count data rather than transformed data to avoid information loss. Then, we use a log-mixture structure to account for cell type composition while simultaneously correcting for the spot and platform effects between ST and scRNA-seq data. To characterize the gene expression profile of each cell type at a spot, we decompose it on the log scale into three components: the average gene expression of the certain cell type, spatial variations, and nonspatial variations.  To handle the above complicated model, we propose a powerful score testing framework that can evaluate the significance of cell-type-specific spatial variations. We first develop an approximate algorithm based on penalized quasi-likelihood (PQL) ( 35 ,  36 ) to fit the null model efficiently. Then, we construct a cell-type-specific test statistic in quadratic form ( 28 ) to examine the significance of the variance component related to spatial locations. This test statistic incorporates a cell-type-specific membership matrix to account for the contributions from individual cell types, effectively addressing the confounding issues arising from the cell type mixtures in the ST data. Since the true expression patterns of genes are largely unknown and can vary across genes and cell types in practice, we use the Cauchy combination method ( 37 ,  38 ) to aggregate the information from diverse spatial kernels that cover a wide spectrum of common spatial patterns observed in real datasets. The technical details are provided in  Materials and Methods , and   SI Appendix ,  Methods  .    Simulation Study. To highlight the essential role of each component in the MMM model, we simulated five scenarios, where Scenarios 1 and 2 were designed to study the influence of cell type mixtures on SVG identification, Scenario 3 was designed to study the spot and platform effects, Scenario 4 combined all the above settings to mimic the real ST data, and Scenario 5 was designed to study the method’s sensitivity to prior assumptions. Specifically, in Scenario 1, the proportions of cell types 1 and 2 were uniformly distributed across space ( Fig. 1 C  ). We found that the    P   -values of MMM and non-cell-type-specific methods were well calibrated in the null case ( Fig. 1 D  ), and all methods could successfully identify SVGs in the alternative case; however, non-cell-type-specific methods could not clarify which cell type the spatial variations belonged to ( Fig. 1 E  ). In Scenario 2, we varied the cell type composition spatially, with the proportion of cell type 1 increasing from left to right and cell type 2 in contrast ( Fig. 1 F  ). Due to the heterogeneity in gene expression profiles between the two cell types, non-cell-type-specific methods identified their respective marker genes as SVGs ( Fig. 1 H  ), while MMM controlled type I errors by accounting for the cell type composition ( Fig. 1 G  ). In Scenario 3, we kept the cell type composition randomly distributed, but varied the spot effects     α  i    ’s spatially ( Fig. 1 I  ) and added gene-specific platform effects     γ  g    ’s ( Fig. 1 J  ). This was designed to examine the robustness of the methods in the presence of batch effects and platform differences. Under the null condition, MMM still produced well-calibrated    P   -values for both cell types by explicitly correcting for these two effects, while Celina yielded slightly inflated results ( Fig. 1 K  ). Celina’s unsatisfactory control of type I errors in this scenario is likely due to its modeling of normalized data instead of raw count data. The data transformation step before analysis can lead to an inadequate characterization of the mean–variance relationship inherent in raw count data and introduce systematic errors ( 23 ,  39 ), thus preventing the full elimination of confounding bias. In Scenario 4, we combined the settings of Scenarios 2 and 3 so that the cell type composition varied spatially, as well as varying spot effects and gene-specific platform effects. We should note that Scenario 4 was the most challenging and also the closest to real ST data. We then set the false discovery rate cutoff at 0.05 and measured the power of MMM and other cell-type-specific methods in the alternative case ( Fig. 1 L  ). We found that MMM was more powerful than the other two methods across all settings of spatial pattern and sample size because of its ability to aggregate information from multiple kernels corresponding to diverse spatial patterns and correction for spot effects and platform effects. Compared to Celina, the power gain of MMM is due to its modeling of raw count data, which avoids the loss of information ( 23 ,  40 ). C-SIDE suffered from low statistical power since its nonparametric mode is not effective in combining the    P   -values corresponding to multiple basis functions (  SI Appendix ,  Methods  ). However, we should emphasize that its performance here does not reflect the effectiveness in the task for which it was originally designed. In Scenario 5, we generated data with varied prior distributions, including “flat top,” “skew,” and “bimodal” ( Fig. 1 M  ), to evaluate whether MMM is sensitive to prior assumptions (more prior settings in   SI Appendix , Fig. S1 ). We examined MMM under the null condition first ( Fig. 1 N  ) and then in the alternative case ( Fig. 1 O  ). The obtained    P   -values were well calibrated in all settings, showing that MMM is robust to prior assumptions. In summary, MMM outperformed all existing methods in various scenarios, both in terms of statistical power and type I error control. MMM Produces Replicable Results Across Multiple Adult Mouse Brain Datasets and Reveals the Heritability Enrichment in Brain-Related Phenotypes.  In this section, we applied MMM to multiple adult mouse brain ST datasets, including two slices profiled by the 10x Visium platform ( 43 ) and a 3D model constructed using 35 slices profiled by Spatial Transcriptomics ( 44 ). By comparing the results from several datasets, we showed MMM’s robustness and consistency across different sources and perspectives. We further showed that the heritability of cell-type-specific SVGs was significantly enriched in certain brain-related traits and diseases. Throughout the study, we used STitch3D to perform cell type deconvolution with a mouse brain snRNA-seq dataset containing 59 cell types ( 27 ) as reference.  We first focused on the two Visium slices of the adult mouse brain across the antero-posterior (AP) axis ( 43 ), which have relatively well-defined morphological characteristics and thus allow a reasonable and distinct comparison ( Fig. 3 A  ). For example, the thalamus is a paired structure of gray matter situated near the brain center, and the hippocampus exhibits consistent thickness and comprises curve-shaped subregions, including three cornu ammonis (CA) areas and the dentate gyrus (DG). Compared to existing methods, the    P   -values obtained from MMM were more consistent between two slices ( Fig. 3 B   and   SI Appendix , Fig. S6 ). Then, we focused on four cell-type-specific SVGs identified by MMM, including Ext_Thal_1-specific SVGs  Pcp4  and  Nrxn3  ( Fig. 3 C  ), and Inh_1-specific SVGs  Calb1  and  Gnas  ( Fig. 3 E  ). We found that their expression variations revealed by MMM within respective cell types showed replicable spatial patterns between the two slices ( Fig. 3  D  and  F  ). Next, we applied MMM to a 3D model constructed from 35 coronal slices of a mouse brain hemisphere along the AP axis. The original dataset was generated by Spatial Transcriptomics technology ( 44 ). A significant challenge in analyzing the 3D model was the presence of batch effects across the numerous slices. However, the cell-type-specific SVGs identified by MMM exhibited spatial patterns that closely aligned with previous findings ( Fig. 3  G  and  H  ). This suggests that MMM is effective in correcting batch effects across the slices. To further demonstrate the robustness of MMM, we evaluated its sensitivity to different deconvolution methods and rotation of spatial coordinates. First, by integrating MMM with estimated cell type proportions by RCTD and STitch3D, respectively, we found that it produced consistent results for most cell types (  SI Appendix , Fig. S7 ). Then, we applied MMM to the two slices rotated by 45 degrees and compared the results before and after rotation, showing its rotational invariance (  SI Appendix , Fig. S8 ). Overall, the cell-type-specific SVG identification results from MMM were stable and reliable in practice.    Fig. 3. In many recent studies, the integration of the risk genetic variants identified by GWASs with other omics data provides valuable insights into mechanisms that underlie complex traits and diseases ( 16 ,  46 – 53 ). For example, the integration of GWAS and scRNA-seq data is a promising way to reveal functional programs and pathogenic processes at the single-cell resolution ( 49 – 52 ). However, the heterogeneity within the same cell type and lack of spatial location information severely limit accurate investigations of cellular origins in the tissue context. Although some methods attempt to utilize the ST data to tackle the above challenges ( 16 ), the common cell type mixtures confound the results and prevent finer resolution analyses. Here, we conducted an integrative analysis of the GWAS summary statistics data from European ancestry with the cell-type-specific SVGs identified by MMM. Unlike the heritability enrichment analysis for highly expressed genes in certain tissues, our analysis provides a unique angle to characterize risk genes within a spatially variable and cell-type-specific context.  To do so, we aligned mouse genes with human genes, which is a commonly adopted strategy for studying human traits and diseases ( 16 ,  46 ,  50 ). Despite the biological differences between humans and mice, arguments in favor of using mouse RNA-seq data have been well discussed ( 50 ). First, gene expression profiles are highly conserved between humans and mice ( 54 ), which is supported by a series of large-scale projects ( 55 – 57 ). Second, high-quality RNA-seq data are more readily obtainable from mice than from humans. Third, the key findings from mouse data have been successfully replicated in human data in previous studies ( 50 ). After aligning mouse genes with human genes, we mapped these genes to single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in the human genome based on reference annotations ( 58 ), and generated a unique set of SNP annotations for each cell type. By treating a cell-type-specific SNP set as the annotation set, we evaluated whether the corresponding cell-type-specific genes can explain a higher proportion of heritability for a phenotype using the stratified linkage disequilibrium score regression (S-LDSC) ( 46 ,  59 ,  60 ). Here, we considered GWAS summary statistics data for 30 phenotypes (  SI Appendix , Table S1 ), which can be roughly grouped into two categories: brain-related, including intelligence (IQ), memory, reaction time (RT), verbal-numerical reasoning (VNR), Alzheimer’s disease (AD), epilepsy, Parkinson’s disease (PD), anorexia nervosa (AN), attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), autism spectrum disorder (ASD), bipolar disorder (BD), cannabis use disorder (CUD), depression, insomnia, obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), obsessive-compulsive symptoms (OCS), posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD), schizophrenia (SCZ), and Tourette syndrome (TS); and non-brain-related, including coronary artery disease (CAD), high blood pressure (HBP), pulse rate (PR), free thyroxine (FT4), thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), type 2 diabetes (T2D), body mass index (BMI), waist-hip ratio (WHR), bone mineral density (BMD), height, and osteoarthritis (OA).  Note that we have two groups of genes for heritability enrichment analysis: cell-type-specific highly expressed genes identified from scRNA-seq reference data and cell-type-specific SVGs identified by MMM in ST data (  SI Appendix , Table S3 ). To differentiate the contributions of two groups of genes, we first examined the heritability enrichment of genes that are highly expressed in each brain cell type. After mapping these brain-expressed genes to the human genome, we conducted S-LDSC using its baseline model, which includes 52 functional categories (such as genic regions, enhancer regions, and conserved regions) along with a category encompassing all SNPs. For each cell type, we incorporated the SNP annotation set derived from cell-type-specific highly expressed genes into the baseline model and estimated their heritability enrichment across the 30 phenotypes. We summarized the results of the enrichment analysis in   SI Appendix , Fig. S9  and observed significant enrichment of these highly expressed genes in most brain-related phenotypes. In contrast, no cell types in this mouse brain study exhibited statistically significant enrichment in non-brain-related traits or diseases, serving as a negative control. To characterize the contribution from cell-type-specific SVGs, we further added an SNP annotation set derived from the cell-type-specific SVGs to the baseline model of S-LDSC, conditional on the cell-type-specific highly expressed gene sets. The results of the heritability enrichment analysis are shown in  Fig. 3 I  . We found that the SVGs of certain neuronal subtypes were significantly enriched in cognitive traits, such as IQ and VNR, as well as in psychiatric disorders, including BD, depression, insomnia, OCD, and TS. This indicates that within these neuronal subtypes, only a subset of cells in specific regions drives the corresponding traits and diseases by regulating the expression of genetics-informed genes. For example,  Nrxn3  was an SVG within Ext_Thal_1 cells ( Fig. 3 D  ) while its human homolog  NRXN3  links synaptic cell adhesion to cognition and its disorders ( 61 – 63 ). Mutations in  NRXN3  may cause developmental delay, learning disability, movement disorder, and behavioral problems ( 64 ,  65 ). We further performed a gene analysis using MAGMA ( 66 ) with GWAS summary statistics data as input and found that  NRXN3  was significantly associated with IQ (adjusted    P   -value     1.284  ×   10   −  4      ). In summary, the cell-type-specific SVGs identified by MMM have great potential to elucidate the mechanisms underlying complex traits and diseases in the spatial context through integrative analysis with GWAS hits.    MMM Yields Robust Results on the 10x Xenium Human Breast Cancer Dataset by Accounting for the Uncertainties in Cell Segmentation and Annotation.  To demonstrate the effectiveness and stability of our method for high-resolution ST data, we applied MMM to a human breast cancer dataset ( 7 ) generated by 10x Xenium, a recently developed imaging-based ST technology that enables measurement of gene expression at the subcellular resolution. The reference data were generated using Chromium Single Cell Gene Expression Flex applied to FFPE tissues (scFFPE-seq) in the same study ( 7 ).  Typically, analyzing the Xenium data at the single-cell level requires two preprocessing steps: cell segmentation ( 67 – 69 ) and cell type annotation ( 70 ,  71 ) ( Fig. 4 A  ), both of which introduce significant uncertainties in the subsequent investigations. For example, in the cell segmentation step, imperfect boundary division can lead to the inclusion of transcripts from surrounding cells into the target cell, thus causing cell mixtures. More importantly, these transcripts may not belong to the target cell type ( Fig. 4 B  ). Second, cell type annotation in a deterministic way can also bring uncertainty due to imperfect segmentation. To demonstrate this, we applied RCTD to estimate the probabilities of the most likely cell type of each cell segmented by UCS ( 69 ). Notably, many cells exhibit a probability of less than 0.75 for their most likely cell type ( Fig. 4 C  ). Ignoring these uncertainties can lead to inflated type I error rates when identifying cell-type-specific SVGs. Moreover, outcomes from different segmentation and annotation methods can vary a lot ( Fig. 4 D  ), posing a huge challenge for reproducibility. Within the MMM framework, we use the log-mixture structure to account for these uncertainties in the probabilistic view, producing consistent    P   -values when using segmented cells from different methods as input ( Fig. 4 E  , first row); in contrast, ignoring these uncertainties may lead to substantially less consistent results ( Fig. 4 E  , second row). MMM Provides Consistent Results Across Multiple Colorectal Cancer Datasets from Different ST Technologies.  To evaluate whether MMM can obtain consistent results between ST data with varied resolutions, we applied MMM to the human colorectal cancer (CRC) datasets ( 8 ) generated by multiple ST technologies, including Visium, Visium HD, and Xenium. Throughout the study, we used the paired scRNA-seq dataset provided in the same study ( 8 ) as reference. We chose the CRC data for two reasons: First, the extreme sparsity and high noise level in the Visium HD data make the analysis particularly challenging, allowing us to highlight MMM’s advantage in statistical power; Second, the paired Visium and Xenium data could be used for verifying the identified cell-type-specific SVGs in the absence of ground truth.  In the tumor boundary region, cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) are often the most abundant stromal cell type, and macrophages are the most abundant immune cell type, both playing crucial roles in shaping the tumor microenvironment (TME). Therefore, we focused on CAFs and macrophages to make the comparison between MMM and existing methods. Since there was no ground truth on cell-type-specific SVGs, we first applied these methods to the Visium HD data and then used the identified cell-type-specific SVGs in the paired Visium data for verification. In the comparison with Celina and C-SIDE, we found that MMM not only identified more cell-type-specific SVGs but also achieved greater consistency between the Visium HD and Visium data (  SI Appendix , Figs. S12 and S13 ). This showed that MMM enjoys higher statistical power when handling sparse and noisy data and thus could obtain more reliable results. We also visualized the spatial patterns of the identified SVGs for CAFs and macrophages using the datasets generated by Visium, Visium HD, and Xenium ( Fig. 5 A  ). We found that the spatial patterns revealed by MMM were highly consistent between different ST technologies. Specifically, MMM identified the colocalization of two subpopulations,  MMP11  +  CAFs and  SPP1  +  macrophages, around the tumor boundary region, providing insights into the tumor microenvironment. High-resolution data have unique advantages when analyzing rare cell types. For example, CD4 +  T cells and CD8 +  cytotoxic T cells are sparsely distributed across the tissue, resulting in very low cell type proportions in the most Visium spots (  SI Appendix , Fig. S14 ). MMM Reveals 3D Spatial Patterns of the Cell-Type-Specific SVGs in the Drosophila Embryo Model Constructed from the Stereo-Seq Dataset.  In this section, we used MMM to analyze a 16 to 18 h  Drosophila  embryo dataset within certain spatial domains to present more distinct spatial patterns of the identified cell-type-specific SVGs in the organ context. The dataset comprises multiple Stereo-seq ST slices ( 81 ), where spatial bins were created by aggregating     20  ×  20     DNA nanoballs into 10 µm    ×    10 µm-sized bins as described in the original study. The reference data were built upon a three-level single-cell combinatorial-indexing RNA-sequencing (sci-RNA-seq3)  Drosophila  embryo atlas ( 82 ) that matches the same developmental stage as the ST data.  We began by applying STitch3D to estimate cell type proportions and reconstruct a 3D whole organism spatial atlas based on 13 ST slices. STitch3D successfully reconstructed the central nervous system (CNS) and salivary gland, which fully recapitulated the morphology and position of the corresponding organ structures ( Fig. 6  A  and  C  ). We then zoomed in on these two specific regions and applied MMM to reveal the spatial patterns of cell-type-specific SVGs in the organ context. Compared to other tasks in which MMM was examined, the detection of cell-type-specific SVGs for the  Drosophila  embryo faced additional challenges. First, the Stereo-seq dataset is highly sparse with more than 95% genes in most spatial bins having zero counts. Second, only a small subset of spots are available for analysis when we focus on a specific region. Both data sparsity and the limited sample size severely restrict statistical power. Moreover, batch differences among multiple ST slices largely confound the results and may cause false discoveries ( Fig. 6  B  and  D   and   SI Appendix , Fig. S15 ). Despite the difficulties, MMM successfully identified cell-type-specific SVGs and enjoyed high statistical power by directly working on raw count data rather than transformed data while simultaneously correcting for slice-specific effects (  SI Appendix ,  Methods  ). We further visualized the expression variations of the identified cell-type-specific SVGs and found that these genes varied significantly at different locations within certain organs ( Fig. 6  B  and  D  ), suggesting that they may correspond to different developmental states or functions. For example,  jim  is an important transcription factor in neuronal diversity ( 83 ) and elimination ( 84 ), and  fabp  overexpression enhances autophagy and suppresses amyloid- pathology, leading to potential therapeutic interventions for Alzheimer’s disease ( 85 ). We also used g:Profiler ( 80 ) to perform a functional enrichment analysis (  SI Appendix , Fig. S16 ). In the analysis of the CNS-specific SVGs, we noted that the GO terms related to CNS development were significantly enriched, such as neuron differentiation (adjusted    P   -value     2.050  ×   10   −  4      ) and generation (adjusted    P   -value     4.979  ×   10   −  4      ). Discussion  Characterizing spatial variations in gene expression with cell type specificity is an important but challenging task for investigating the landscape of complex biological systems in ST studies. In this paper, we have presented MMM, a unified statistical framework for identifying cell-type-specific SVGs in ST datasets. The success of MMM relies on its three carefully designed features. First, MMM uses a log-mixture structure to decompose the measured gene expression at each spot into a linear combination of fractions attributed to different cell types on the log scale, so that the cell-type-specific SVG identification results will not be dominated by the marker genes of certain cell types. Second, MMM explicitly corrects for platform differences between ST and scRNA-seq data, which are commonly found in real data. In contrast, overlooking this difference can lead to misidentification of spatial variations. Third, MMM can aggregate the information across multiple kernels corresponding to various spatial patterns. Therefore, the overall assessment output by MMM is effective in detecting unknown and potentially diverse spatial patterns in real ST data. Through comprehensive numerical experiments, we showed that MMM enjoys high statistical power while appropriately controlling type I error. We also used MMM to analyze eight publicly available ST datasets of different tissues generated from various platforms with a wide range of resolutions. The experimental results indicate that even for high-resolution ST data, considering cell type mixtures contributes to obtaining more stable, reliable, and replicable results. MMM is also easily applicable to 3D datasets, providing more biological insights from the 3D perspective.  MMM directly models the raw RNA counts to avoid information loss, resulting in an appreciable power gain ( 23 ,  40 ). In contrast, ignoring the count nature of ST data can lead to an inadequate characterization of the mean–variance relationship and introduce systematic errors ( 23 ,  39 ). Since the normal distribution cannot approximate the sparse data appropriately, such a power gain is apparent in data with low counts, especially for the recently developed high-resolution ST technologies like Stereo-seq and Visium HD. However, when handling data with high counts, the Gaussian approximation approach is attractive since a more computationally efficient algorithm can be derived.  Finally, we discuss the limitations and potential extensions of MMM. First, MMM requires annotated scRNA-seq data for reference-based deconvolution of cell types. The quality of scRNA-seq reference data and how well it matches the ST data have a notable influence on the deconvolution results and, subsequently, on the cell-type-specific SVG identification. Although single-cell atlases are increasingly available, they may contain missing cell types or substantial platform effects. More importantly, some ST tissues may lack the corresponding scRNA-seq reference data. Second, the cell types of interest may be present in extremely low quantities, which can make MMM unreliable for such rare cell types due to limited sample sizes and significant confounding effects from other cell types mixed together. These limitations may not be reflected in simulations because of the idealized settings of cell type composition but have essential impacts in practice as shown in our analysis of the Visium adult mouse brain dataset (  SI Appendix , Fig. S7 ). Third, while our nonparametric statistical testing framework makes MMM powerful in characterizing general spatial gene expression patterns, their clear biological interpretations still rely on specific scientific questions and further investigations, as illustrated in our real data analyses. Compared to the methods that work on the predefined covariates, such as C-SIDE and niche-DE (  SI Appendix ,  Methods  ), MMM is more suitable for preliminary exploration in cases where prior understanding of ST data is limited. Fourth, MMM was designed to capture spatially correlated cellular heterogeneity by considering each gene separately. However, combining all genes together could provide gene-set-level information. For example, representing the variations of spots across all genes through the low-rank approximation ( 86 – 89 ) generates interpretable factors that can provide deeper biological insights, such as the identification of metagenes, and gene–gene covariation and coregulation analysis.    Materials and Methods   The MMM Method.  Let     Y  =    Y   i  ,  g     ∈    N    I  ×  G       denote the observed gene expression count matrix with the spot index     i  ∈   1  ,  ⋯  ,  I      and the gene index     g  ∈   1  ,  ⋯  ,  G     . To account for cell type mixtures, we first need to determine the cell type proportions       β   i   =     β   i  ,  1    ,  ⋯  ,   β   i  ,  K      T    ∈    R   K      of each spot    i   , where    K    represents the total number of cell types. This can be estimated using deconvolution methods ( 26 ,  34 ) with the paired scRNA-seq data as reference. We further introduce two effects, denoted as      α   =    α  i    ∈    R   I      and      γ  g   ∈  R    , to account for spot-specific effects and gene-specific platform effects between ST and scRNA-seq data. Specifically,     α     captures the variations in total transcript counts between spots while     γ  g     accounts for the expression differences of gene    g    between scRNA-seq and ST platforms. As we are interested in cell-type-specific spatial gene expression patterns, we next introduce the cell-type-specific gene expression profiles       η    i  ,  g    =     η   i  ,  1  ,  g    ,  ⋯  ,   η   i  ,  K  ,  g      T    ∈    R   K      for spot    i   . Then, we consider the following hierarchical probabilistic model ( 26 ,  90 ) for the observed RNA counts in ST data:   [1]         Y   i  ,  g    ∣   λ   i  ,  g        ∼   Poisson    N  i    λ   i  ,  g     ,          [2]        log    λ   i  ,  g         =   x  i   T      ξ   g   +  log     ∑   k  =  1   K     β   i  ,  k     η   i  ,  k  ,  g     +   α  i   +   γ  g   ,         where     N  i     is the total transcript count for spot    i   ,     λ   i  ,  g      represents the underlying expression level of gene    g    for spot    i   ,      x  i   =     x   i  ,  1    ,  ⋯  ,   x   i  ,  C      T    ∈    R   C      is the covariate vector, and       ξ   g   =     ξ   1  ,  g    ,  ⋯  ,   ξ   C  ,  g      T    ∈    R   C      is the vector of corresponding fixed effects shared by all spots. The log-mixture structure (Eq.   2  ) separates the contributions of different cell types by representing     λ   i  ,  g      as the weighted sum of    K    cell-type-specific gene expressions     η   i  ,  k  ,  g     ’s after adjusting for the multiplicative effects      x  i   T      ξ   g     ,     α  i    , and     γ  g    . To characterize cell-type-specific gene expression profiles, we decompose     η   i  ,  k  ,  g      into three components ( 15 ,  23 ) on its log scale as   [3]        log   η   i  ,  k  ,  g    =     log   η   0  ,  k  ,  g     ⏟    log mean expression    +     b   i  ,  k  ,  g    ⏟    spatial variation    +     ϵ   i  ,  k  ,  g    ⏟    nonspatial variation    ,         where     log   η   0  ,  k  ,  g       is the logarithm of mean expression of cell type    k   , calculated from scRNA-seq data. The term     b   i  ,  k  ,  g      captures the cell-type-specific spatial correlation pattern among spots at different locations, and     ϵ   i  ,  k  ,  g      represents nonspatial variation. Given the mixed-effects model (Eq.   3  ), we now focus on how to distinguish the spatial variation term from the nonspatial variation term. For gene    g   , we use a stationary Gaussian process to characterize the spatial variations from the same cell type    k    across all spots and an independent and identical Gaussian prior for all nonspatial variations ( 23 )   [4]           b   1  ,  k  ,  g    ,  ⋯  ,   b   I  ,  k  ,  g      T    ∼  N   0  ,   τ   k  ,  g    K   ,    ϵ   i  ,  k  ,  g    ∼  N   0  ,   τ   ϵ  ,  g     ,         where matrix     K  ∈    R    I  ×  I       is a prespecified kernel function of the spatial locations      ℓ   =      ℓ   1   ,  ⋯  ,    ℓ   I     T       with the     (  i  ,   i  ′   )    -th element being      K   i  ,   i  ′     =  K     ℓ   i   ,    ℓ    i  ′       ,     τ   k  ,  g      is the scaling factor of spatial variance component, and     τ   ϵ  ,  g      is the variance of nonspatial variance component. In contrast to existing methods, our formulation presents several unique advantages for characterizing spatial gene expression patterns in a cell-type-specific manner. First, we begin the model design with raw count data rather than transformed data to avoid information loss. Second, the log-mixture structure (Eq.   2  ) accounts for cell type composition while simultaneously correcting for the spot and platform effects between ST and scRNA-seq data. Third, the mixed-effects model (Eq.   3  ) enables a statistically rigorous way to examine the significance of spatial variations. Furthermore, our model can be extended to identify cell-type-specific SVGs in the multiple slices case and allow for batch effect correction by modeling the slice-specific effects (  SI Appendix ,  Methods  ). In summary, these features enable MMM to seamlessly integrate with the count-based deconvolution methods, establishing it as a unified framework for identifying cell-type-specific SVGs.  To determine whether gene    g    is an SVG of cell type    k   , we can formulate it as a statistical testing problem with the null hypothesis      H  0   :   τ   k  ,  g    =  0     against the alternative one      H  1   :   τ   k  ,  g    >  0    . To evaluate the significance of the spatial variance component of each cell type, we propose a powerful score testing framework while considering the cell type mixtures. Specifically, we first develop an approximate algorithm based on PQL ( 35 ,  36 ) to fit the null model efficiently. After the algorithm converges, we obtain the pseudo data vector       Y  ~   g   ∈    R   I      in the linear mixed-effects form with the marginal distribution       Y  ~   g   ∼  N   X    ξ   g   ,    Σ   g       under the null condition. Here,     X  =     x  1   ,  ⋯  ,   x  I     T    ∈    R    I  ×  C       is the covariate matrix of all spots,       Σ   g   =   W  g   −  1    +   ∑   k  =  1   K    M   k  ,  g      τ   ϵ  ,  g    I    M   k  ,  g    T       is the covariance matrix,      W  g   ∈    R    I  ×  I       is the diagonal weight matrix, and      M   k  ,  g    ∈    R    I  ×  I       is the membership matrix indicating the contribution of cell type    k    to each spot. Motivated by the marginal distribution of pseudo data, we construct a cell-type-specific test statistic in quadratic form ( 28 )   [5]         Q   k  ,  g    =   1  2      P  g     Y  ~   g     T      M   k  ,  g    K   M   k  ,  g    T       P  g     Y  ~   g    ,         which follows a mixture of     χ  1  2     distributions under the null hypothesis. Here,     P  g     is the symmetric projection matrix defined as      P  g   =    Σ   g   −  1    −    Σ   g   −  1    X     X   T      Σ   g   −  1    X    −  1     X   T      Σ   g   −  1      . Note that     M   k  ,  g      contains cell-type-specific information to help address the confounding issue due to the mixture of cell types. The power of the above hypothesis testing scheme is obviously determined by how well the kernel matrix    K    matches the true spatial variations exhibited by the gene of interest within a certain cell type. Hence, we use the Cauchy combination method ( 38 ) to aggregate information from multiple kernels capturing various spatial patterns and calculate a calibrated    P   -value as the overall assessment. The technical details are provided in   SI Appendix ,  Methods  .    Seamless Integration with Cell Type Deconvolution.  Through our numerical experiments, we found that the cell type proportions estimated by the deconvolution methods play an important role in the cell-type-specific SVG identification, and thus keeping the deconvolution and SVG models consistent in terms of the definition of cell type proportion is essential to controlling the false positive rates and yielding reliable and interpretable results. Within the MMM model, cell type proportion     β   i  ,  k      represents the ratio of the transcript count from cell type    k    to all transcripts at spot    i   . Here, we highlight its difference with another definition based on the number of cells rather than transcripts. Therefore, we chose RCTD ( 26 ) and STitch3D ( 34 ) to estimate the cell type proportions for MMM throughout the study. Specifically, we used RCTD for the single ST slice case and STitch3D for the multiple ST slices case. For a fair comparison in simulation studies, we used RCTD for C-SIDE ( 15 ) and CARD ( 33 ) for Celina ( 31 ) as suggested in their tutorial websites. The above deconvolution methods all require the ST data with paired scRNA-seq data as input.  MMM offers a seamless integration with the results from the deconvolution step. For example, the cell type proportion     β   i  ,  k     , spot-specific effect     α  i    , and gene-specific platform effect     γ  g     can be directly inherited from the cell type deconvolution step. After plugging in these estimates, no identifiable issue exists when fitting the MMM model. While the first two are necessary (    β   i  ,  k      and     α  i    ), users can choose not to provide the platform effect     γ  g    , and our software would estimate it automatically by adding a column of ones in the covariate matrix    X    and treating     γ  g     as an intercept term. Comparing to fixing     γ  g     the same as the deconvolution result, we observed better model fits by leaving it unconstrained in practice. The reason can be that the deconvolution model may not be exactly the same as the SVG model, and the latter fitted one should therefore be more appropriate. As a result, we allow     γ  g     to be a free parameter in our software.    Computational Efficiency.  We analyze the computational complexity of the MMM method to assess its scalability. Given the RNA count matrix     Y  ∈    N    I  ×  G       containing    I    sample spots and    G    genes, we focus on one gene at a time since all genes can be processed in parallel in our software implementation. To fit the null model, the MMM algorithm requires     O    I  2       computations. In the statistical testing step, we need     O    I  2       computations to evaluate the test statistics. Therefore, the overall computations are quadratic to the sample size    I    and linear to the number of genes    G   .  We implemented the MMM method in the open-source R package MCube, which employs a carefully designed parallel computing framework to achieve high scalability and efficient memory control with user-configurable parameters. Notably, users can flexibly specify the number of worker processes along with the number of threads on Basic Linear Algebra Subprograms per worker. This hierarchical control empowers the maximal utilization of available computational resources. In addition, to address memory constraints inherent in large-scale kernel matrix operations, we handle matrices that are too large to load in memory through memory-mapping to binary files on disk ( 91 ). This approach enables the kernel matrices that exceed physical memory limits while maintaining efficient data access.  We also conducted a runtime benchmark on simulated datasets (  SI Appendix , Fig. S2 ) and recorded the computation time for all the real data analyses (  SI Appendix , Table S7 ). evidence_text:
Randomized Spatial PCA (RASP): A computationally efficient method for dimensionality reduction of high-resolution spatial transcriptomics data. Spatial transcriptomics (ST) provides critical insights into the spatial organization of gene expression, enabling researchers to unravel the intricate relationship between cellular environments and biological function. Identifying spatial domains within tissues is key to understanding tissue architecture and mechanisms underlying development and disease progression. Here, we present Randomized Spatial PCA (RASP), a novel spatially-aware dimensionality reduction method for ST data. RASP is designed to be orders-of-magnitude faster than existing techniques, scale to datasets with 100,000+ locations, support flexible integration of non-transcriptomic covariates, and reconstruct de-noised, spatially-smoothed gene expression values. RASP itself is not a clustering or domain detection method; cell types and spatial regions are obtained by clustering the RASP PCs, and the effective cluster resolution depends on the K-nearest-neighbor (kNN) graph and a smoothing parameter β. It employs a randomized two-stage PCA framework and configurable spatial smoothing. RASP was compared to BASS, GraphST, SEDR, SpatialPCA, STAGATE, and CellCharter using diverse ST datasets (10x Visium, Stereo-Seq, MERFISH, 10x Xenium) on human and mouse tissues. In these benchmarks, RASP delivers comparable or superior accuracy in tissue-domain detection while achieving substantial improvements in computational speed. Its efficiency not only reduces runtime and resource requirements but also makes it practical to explore a broad range of spatial-smoothing parameters in a high-throughput fashion. By enabling rapid re-analysis under different parameter settings, RASP empowers users to fine-tune the balance between resolution and noise suppression on large, high-resolution subcellular datasets-a critical capability when investigating complex tissue architecture. 1 Introduction  Spatial transcriptomics (ST) assays measure gene expression at thousands to hundreds-of-thousands of spatial locations within tissue sections, enabling researchers to characterize transcript abundance  in vivo  at resolutions ranging from small cell groups to subcellular structures [ 1 , 2 ]. ST technology facilitates exploration of gene expression’s spatial organization, providing insights into cellular microenvironments and functional states of individual cells [ 3 ]. Two primary types of ST technologies exist: high-throughput sequencing technologies (sST) and single-molecule fluorescent in situ hybridization or imaging-based technologies (iST) [ 4 , 5 ]. High-throughput sequencing technologies, such as 10x Genomics’ Visium, capture mRNA transcripts at multiple sites or spots on a slide. The original 10x Visium platform offers a resolution of 55 μm, with each spot containing between 1–10 cells [ 6 ]. Emerging technologies, such as Visium HD, promise higher resolution of 2 μm, approaching single-cell levels, while alternatives like Slide-seq V2 capture transcripts with a resolution of 10 μm, also nearing single-cell resolution [ 7 , 8 ]. iST technologies, which reach single cell resolution, include platforms such as MERFISH/MERSCOPE (Vizgen), seqFISH, osmFISH, COsMx, and 10x Xenium [ 9 – 13 ]. A notable advancement in recent years has been the introduction of iST platforms that support the use of formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tissue samples, allowing for use of archival tissue banks, increasing the use of iST technologies [ 9 , 12 , 13 ]. Additionally, probe sets used in iST technologies have expanded, with systems like 10x Xenium developing probe sets with up to 5,000 individual probes [ 14 ], helping to bridge the trade-off between sequencing depth and resolution, allowing for more comprehensive profiling of gene expression. As costs decrease and technology advances, ST studies will transition from analyzing small sample sizes to extensive investigations [ 2 , 13 , 15 – 19 ], generating multi-slide, multi-timepoint ST datasets covering millions of cells across tissues [ 2 ]. Larger datasets necessitate development of novel computational tools that leverage both spatial and transcriptomic data efficiently.  ST’s rich data allows tissue investigation at multiple biological scales, and computational approaches must adapt. On a cellular level, cell type assignment facilitates spatial distribution visualization, enhancing understanding of cellular structure and function in native tissue [ 20 , 21 ]. At larger scales, identifying tissue domains aids comprehension of complex tissue microenvironments. Identifying cell types and spatial domains is achievable with recently developed computational tools. Popular single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) tools like Seurat and Scanpy perform principal component analysis (PCA) and clustering on gene expression data while disregarding spatial context [ 22 , 23 ]. However, methods like BASS and FICT now incorporate spatial context [ 24 , 25 ]. For spatial domain detection, methodologies like BASS, SEDR, GraphST, STAGATE, SpatialPCA, CellCharter, Banksy, NichePCA, and MENDER exist [ 24 , 26 – 33 ], utilizing different model architectures to embed spatial and gene expression data into low-dimensionality spaces for clustering and domain identification. ST data is often sparse, so de-noising and imputing poorly captured transcripts is a desirable feature, and many spatially-aware methods provide this functionality [ 34 – 37 ].  Yet, current methods have notable limitations. While effective on a single ST slice with few profiled locations, they are computationally intensive, exhibiting slow processing locally, particularly on iST datasets exceeding 100,000 cells. With iST dataset generation increasing, efficient, spatially-aware dimensionality reduction algorithms are necessary. Many existing methods are also inflexible and complex, hindering customization of spatial smoothing or integration of non-transcriptomic covariates, such as those derived from hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) images or protein abundance metrics. Addressing these limitations is crucial for deriving meaningful insights from large-scale ST datasets.  In this paper, we present Randomized Spatial PCA (RASP), a computational method for fast, scalable, and interpretable spatially aware dimensionality reduction. RASP produces spatially smoothed principal components (PCs) and optionally reconstructs de-noised, spatially smoothed gene expression values. Importantly, RASP is not a clustering or domain detection method; cell types and spatial domains are obtained by clustering the RASP PCs with standard algorithms (e.g., Leiden/Louvain or Gaussian mixtures). The effective resolution of the resulting clusters depends on the K-nearest-neighbor (kNN) graph used to define spatial neighborhoods and a smoothing parameter  β  that controls the strength of spatial regularization. RASP employs randomized linear algebra for efficient dimensionality reduction of large datasets [ 38 ], supports integration of covariates such as cellular density or sequencing depth, and exposes the kNN and  β  parameters to enable user-controlled smoothing. Tested on six real-world and two simulated datasets (including 10x Genomics Visium/Visium HD and subcellular imaging technologies like Stereo-Seq, MERFISH, and 10x Xenium), pipelines that cluster RASP PCs exhibit tissue-domain concordance comparable to or better than existing methods, with competitive runtimes. This efficiency facilitates systematic exploration of kNN and  β  to balance resolution and noise suppression in large, high-resolution datasets.    2 Results   2.1 RASP overview  RASP performs dimensionality reduction and spatial smoothing on normalized ST data, with the option to incorporate location-specific covariates. The randomized two-stage PCA optimizes computational efficiency while enabling the flexible and efficient analysis of high-resolution ST datasets. RASP utilizes a sparse matrix representation of the data, conducts dimensionality reduction via randomized PCA, and generates spatially smoothed principal components (PCs) using an inverse distance matrix sparsified by a kNN threshold ( Fig 1A ). Covariates integration into the latent variables is achieved through an optional second-stage randomized PCA on a matrix with covariates appended to first-stage smoothed PCs. RASP’s spatially smoothed PCs are useful for a variety of downstream analyses, including clustering and reduced rank reconstruction of gene-level expression. See Algorithm 1 and  Sect 4.1  for details. Note that by default, RASP utilizes 20 PCs, although this is a user tunable parameter. See Figs O and P in  S1 Text  for effects of variable PC number on RASP performance.   10.1371/journal.pcbi.1013759.g001  Fig 1   RASP overview.   A: Method workflow.  RASP takes as input a cell-by-gene expression matrix and spatial coordinates from a ST experiment. The expression matrix is reduced via randomized PCA and spatially smoothed by a sparse inverse distance matrix. Non-transcriptomic covariates can be added at this stage (not pictured). The output of RASP can be used for downsteam analyses including cell type annotation and spatial domain identification.  B: Evaluation pipeline.  RASP was tested on four ST datasets each generated using a different platform (MERFISH, Stereo-seq, Xenium, Visium) and two synthetic datasets (100 replicates each). RASP results were compared against standard PCA and alternative spatially aware dimensionality reduction models (SEDR, GraphST, SpatialPCA, BASS, STAGATE, CellCharter, nichePCA, and MENDER) for both accuracy and speed.                        2.2 RASP evaluation on real data  We applied RASP to six publicly available ST datasets generated using diverse techniques and resolutions on human and mouse tissues including the mouse ovary (Vizgen MERFISH technology), mouse olfactory bulb (STOmics Stereo-seq technology), human breast cancer tumor (10x Genomics, Xenium technology), human DLPFC (10x Genomics, Visium technology), and Sagittal mouse brain (Allen institute, Vizgen MERFISH technology), and Coronal mouse brain (10x Genomics, Visium HD technology) ( Fig 1B ) and Table A in  S1 Text . For details regarding field standard preprocessing steps used, such as filtering criteria and normalization, please refer to  Sects 4.4.1 – 4.4.3 , and Sect 1.2 in  S1 Text , Sect 1.3 in  S1 Text .  We evaluated RASP by clustering locations using the spatially smoothed principal components (PCs) output by the algorithm. Cluster quality was assessed through spatial continuity and compactness via CHAOS score (Sect 1.3 in  S1 Text ), spatial autocorrelation by Moran’s I (Sect 1.4 in  S1 Text ) and the Adjusted Rand Index (ARI) (Sect 1.2 in  S1 Text ) compared to ground truth annotations. We conducted a sensitivity analysis on key RASP parameters, focusing on the kNN distance threshold for sparse matrix construction and the  β  power parameter (see  Fig 1A ). This analysis used a one-parameter-at-a-time strategy to investigate parameter impacts on clustering outcomes.  Performance comparisons were made between RASP and eight other spatially informed dimensionality reduction or spatial domain detection methods: GraphST [ 26 ], SEDR [ 27 ], SpatialPCA [ 28 ], STAGATE [ 29 ], CellCharter [ 30 ], nichePCA [ 32 ],MENDER [ 33 ], and the joint cell type and domain inference tool BASS [ 24 ], as well as performing randomized PCA. For each comparison, we adhered to the respective GitHub tutorials to run these methods for spatial domain and cell type detection. Clustering of latent dimensions found by each method was performed using Mclust [ 39 ], Louvain [ 40 ], Leiden [ 41 ], and Walktrap [ 42 ] algorithms, where appropriate. For datasets with ground truth annotations, the ARI values presented are based on a default range of parameters outlined in  Table 1 .   10.1371/journal.pcbi.1013759.t001  Table 1   RASP parameter suggestions. Obtained from Huang et al., [ 15 ] it includes ground truth cell type annotations based on histology and differential gene expression ( Fig 2A ). Annotations include luteal, luteinizing mural, granulosa, theca, and stromal cells, with clear spatial organization, alongside endothelial, epithelial, and immune cells, which are heterogeneously distributed across the tissue [ 43 ], making automatic annotation challenging.   10.1371/journal.pcbi.1013759.g002  Fig 2   Overview of mouse ovary analysis using Vizgen MERFISH data.
